extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and school mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for teaching and designing classroom activities to foster students' deductive reasoning and proof abilities in school mathematics, informed by Johnson-Laird's mental models theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of statements accepted by the classroom community
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs should use statements accepted by the classroom community (set of accepted statements) that are true and available without further justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of accepted statements include definitions, axioms, theorems. Instruction should make explicit which statements are treated as available so students need not justify them again when constructing proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ forms of reasoning valid and within students' conceptual reach
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs must employ modes of argumentation that are valid and known to, or within the conceptual reach of, the classroom community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity here means supporting logically necessary inferences from premises; instructors should ensure students know and can apply the forms of reasoning expected at their level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate proofs in appropriate and accessible modes of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs must be communicated with forms of expression (modes of argument representation) that are appropriate and known to, or within the conceptual reach of, the classroom community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modes include verbal, pictorial, algebraic, etc. Choice of representation should match students' familiarity and support understanding rather than impose unfamiliar formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive reasoning must support logically necessary inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive reasoning corresponds to modes of argumentation that need to be valid and therefore support logically necessary inferences from a given set of premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notion of deductive reasoning is independent of whether the representation is formal or informal; emphasis is on logical necessity of the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct mental models of the premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoners should construct a mental model of the information presented in the premises—a mental representation whose structure is analogous to the situation it represents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction can support students in translating premises into internal models (or external sketches) that mirror relations among terms; success depends on linguistic comprehension of premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scan models for informative true conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: After constructing a model, reasoners should scan it for an informative conclusion that is true given the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should help students practice identifying conclusions that follow from their models rather than leaping to hasty or unexamined claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for alternative models (seek counterexamples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoners should search for alternative mental models that may refute the tentative conclusion—i.e., actively look for counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should emphasize validation via searching for alternative models; failure to consider alternatives (often due to memory limits) leads to errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop linguistic competence with logical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must develop competence in understanding logical terms (e.g., and, or, not, if, none, some, all, quantifiers) to construct appropriate models from premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developmental constraints are important (e.g., young children often misinterpret quantifiers); explicit teaching of logical vocabulary is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for working memory limitations when designing tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: The difficulty of deductive tasks depends on the number of models to be constructed and the figural arrangement of terms; working memory capacity constrains the ability to hold and manipulate models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks mindful of processing load: avoid forcing students to hold many alternative models simultaneously; recognize that time pressure reduces performance to younger-learner levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent unnecessary working memory usage through scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruction should prevent unnecessary usage of students' working memory when they engage with proving tasks (for example, by specifying a small set of relevant premises).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scaffolded proving tasks that exclude irrelevant premises free cognitive resources to focus on logical structure and ideas; such scaffolds are especially useful in early stages of proof learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach strategies for effective management of working memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Help students develop strategies (cognitive and representational) to manage working memory while solving proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended strategies include reformulating premises into more concise equivalent forms (e.g., algebraic expressions) and using external records to offload memory demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promote use of concise equivalent representations (e.g., algebraic reformulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing premises in equivalent, concise, and easier-to-manage forms reduces processing load and facilitates construction and manipulation of models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reformulating 'multiple of 3' and 'multiple of 6' definitions as 3l and 6k helped derive the result more easily; encourage algebraic or symbolic reformulations where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual records/diagrams to integrate information
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage making efficient use of visual records (diagrams) to integrate disparate sources of information and reduce working memory demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should teach students how to integrate givens with diagrams (particularly in geometry) rather than treating them separately, since mental integration is cognitively demanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide practice to improve deductive reasoning and internalize proof structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice on deductive tasks can lead to spontaneous improvement in reasoning ability and can help students internalize the general logical structure of proof methods (e.g., proof by contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings show measurable gains without feedback from retesting; practice can make use of automatized elements of proof so working memory can be freed for higher-level reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach selection of relevant premises from the community's accepted statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need to learn to select a collection of relevant premises (from definitions, theorems, axioms) when tasks present only a prompt and not an explicit set of givens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should include tasks where students must identify and justify which accepted statements are relevant, since many real proving tasks require this selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ritualized emphasis on form that obscures logical substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overemphasizing ritual or formal surface structure (e.g., two-column proofs) in ways that cause students to practice form rather than the logical, coherent chain of reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical two-column practice turned proof into rote ritual; instead emphasize sense-making and the logical connections between statements and reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster meta-cognitive reflection on one's reasoning performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop students' meta-ability to reflect on their own performance as part of the developmental gains in deductive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage reflection about model construction, checks for counterexamples, and strategy choices so students improve monitoring and regulation of their reasoning processes.
